title: Loudcasting: Is it ever OK to go headphone free in public?
description:
There’s a name for when people blare out music, scroll through social media on full volume or talk on loudspeaker in public - loudcasting. Surveys show that in the U.K. most adults find this behaviour irritating, but there’s also data suggesting that your age and culture may influence how indifferent you are to this kind of noise. BBC Reporter Angus Thompson tells us what experts say and explains why some people get so annoyed. Plus we hear from our friends across the World Service about loudcasting in their country.

summaryZh: 本集探討「 loudcasting 」——在公共場合大聲播放音樂或影片，或用免提講電話的行為。主持人 Hannah Gelbart 與 BBC 記者 Angus Thompson 討論為何這類噪音容易惹人厭：一來科技無所不在，佔據了人們的休息時間；二來我們對環境聲音會習慣化，但手機片段短促且不規則，特別令人生厭。英國通訊辦公室 2022 年調查訪問約一千多人，發現 13 至 17 歲族群約 83% 會在公共場合不戴耳機播放影片，而 55 歲以上較不容忍此行為。節目也引述各地經驗：泰國的 BTS SkyTrain 張貼勿喧嘩等規定、奈及利亞與墨西哥在大眾運輸上常見大聲播放或街頭表演，而香港地鐵可罰款 HK$2000，約 $250 或 £190。來賓建議以禮貌提醒或依賴明確的共同規範與告示來處理。製作團隊包含製作人 William Lee Adams 和 Benita Barden，剪輯 Verity Wilde。
summaryEn: The episode looks at “loudcasting” — playing music or videos loudly in public or taking calls on speaker. Presenter Hannah Gelbart and reporter Angus Thompson explain why it annoys people: pervasive technology, habituation to ambient sounds, and the unpredictable, attention-grabbing snippets from phones. A 2022 Ofcom survey found about 83% of 13–17 year‑olds admit playing videos in public without headphones, while older adults (55+) are less tolerant. The programme compares cultural differences (Thailand discourages loud noise on the BTS SkyTrain; loudcasting is common in parts of Nigeria and Mexico) and notes Hong Kong’s metro can fine offenders HK$2000 (about $250/£190). People often hesitate to confront loudcasters; polite requests, signage and shared norms are suggested. Producers: William Lee Adams and Benita Barden; editor: Verity Wilde.
